title: Justice capacity depends on infrastructure, management, geography, and adjacent services as much as headline spending
source_unit: Institute for Fiscal Studies, Transforming Justice programme, Resources and the justice system
geography: England and Wales justice system, with local-authority and service-distribution analysis

observations.period: 2002–03 to 2028–29; justice-system public spending and capacity

denominator.unit: IFS mid-grant synthesis report covering the Ministry of Justice and associated justice-system resources

current_budget.unit: £ billions of Ministry of Justice day-to-day spending in 2025–26

early_cut.unit: percent real-terms reduction in Ministry of Justice day-to-day budget between 2007–08 and 2016–17

per_person_gap.unit: percent below 2002–03 spending per person in 2025–26

resource_mechanism.value: Funding interacts with infrastructure, management, staff, buildings, providers, demand, and coordination; spending alone does not determine performance

observations.method: Synthesis of IFS economic and administrative studies across justice spending, tribunals, courts, policing, legal aid, and prevention.
observations.uncertainty: The report combines studies at different stages and does not provide one causal estimate of spending on overall justice outcomes; aggregate budgets conceal allocation and productivity differences.
observations.subgroup: People using courts, tribunals, legal aid, policing, prisons, probation, and related public services, with unequal exposure by place and legal problem.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher spending may not improve outcomes if additional inputs are poorly allocated or bottlenecked by staff, buildings, case preparation, management, or demand growth.

denominator.unit: open cases in party-to-state tribunals in early 2026

asylum_immigration_wait.unit: average weeks from receipt to disposal for asylum and immigration appeals in early 2026

social_security_wait.unit: average weeks from receipt to disposal for social-security appeals in early 2026

historical_comparison.value: Asylum and immigration waits rose from 23 weeks in 2013; social-security waits rose from 18 weeks

demand_capacity.value: Backlogs appear driven mainly by case inflows rising faster than resolution capacity, rather than a recent collapse in productivity

observations.method: Analysis of administrative tribunal receipts, disposals, outstanding caseloads, and waiting-time statistics.
observations.uncertainty: Waits describe resolved cases and may not represent the experience of cases still open; the report does not identify the causal contribution of each policy or staffing change.
observations.subgroup: People appealing immigration, asylum, disability-benefit, and other state decisions, often during high-stakes income or status transitions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Improved appeal access or more accurate first-instance decisions could increase receipts while improving substantive justice, so rising caseload is not itself proof of system failure.

observations.period: 2013–2024; civil legal aid and geographic availability

denominator.unit: England and Wales civil legal-aid system and local-authority distribution

case_volume_change.unit: percent decline in civil legal-aid case volumes by 2024 compared with pre-reform levels

real_expenditure_change.unit: percent decline in real civil legal-aid expenditure by 2024 compared with pre-reform levels

deprivation_pattern.value: Activity fell by roughly 40–65% across the deprivation distribution, with larger absolute losses in places that started with higher likely legal need

need_supply_boundary.value: Lower completed legal-aid cases cannot be read as lower legal need because eligibility, provider viability, fees, and capacity also determine observed activity

observations.method: Analysis of civil legal-aid case volumes, expenditure, provider numbers, local-authority deprivation, and geographic distribution before and after LASPO.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not isolate LASPO causally from other changes or observe all unmet legal need; provider activity is an imperfect measure of effective access.
observations.subgroup: People with housing, welfare, immigration, asylum, debt, family, and public-authority legal problems, especially in deprived local authorities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some decline in completed cases could reflect changed case mix, earlier settlement, or fewer eligible matters rather than only unmet demand, although the available indicators do not resolve the distinction.

observations.period: 2010–2019 and longer-run policy spillovers; courts, police, youth services, and prevention

denominator.unit: IFS synthesis of linked justice and adjacent-service studies

court_closures.unit: magistrates’ court sites closed in England and Wales between 2010 and 2019

police_station_route.value: The geographic allocation and closure of police infrastructure can shape police performance and crime outcomes

adjacent_services.value: Sure Start and youth-club studies indicate that non-justice services can alter later justice demand and wider outcomes

system_interdependence.value: Justice capacity is a cross-service system: prevention, schools, youth provision, police, courts, legal aid, prisons, and probation can shift pressure across one another

observations.method: Synthesis of administrative, geographic, quasi-experimental, and linked-service studies cited by the IFS Transforming Justice programme.
observations.uncertainty: The examples are specific studies and do not establish that every non-justice spending change has the same effect; several pathways remain open or indirect.
observations.subgroup: Residents of areas with different court, police, youth-service, early-years, and legal-aid access; children and young people exposed to preventive services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Service closure or spending changes may coincide with urban restructuring, changing demand, or other reforms, and observed justice effects may not be attributable to one service alone.

related_sources.claim: IFS Transforming Justice programme page and linked component studies.
Component analysis of civil legal-aid provision and geography.

boundary: This record adds justice as public capacity and household-access infrastructure. It covers England and Wales and combines budget, administrative, geographic, and linked-service evidence; it does not produce one causal spending estimate, measure all unmet legal need, equate case volume with justice quality, or generalize UK justice findings to other jurisdictions.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: IFS report reviewed for executive resource findings, tribunal backlogs and waits, legal-aid volume/expenditure/geography, court closures, and cross-service prevention spillovers.
